title: Easily upgradable
text: Got this as a prime day deal at a great price, but it's a nice deal even at the retail price. At minimum the memory should be upgraded to really make this a great machine, the cheapest upgrade is a single 4GB DDR4-2400 memory stick that would double the memory and enable dial channel operation for a nice performance boost. It works great with Linux as long as you stick with the latest kernels, the stock Debian/buster 4.19 kernel had some issues, but it works perfectly with the 5.2 kernel. Despite being a slim lightweight laptop with a large and bright screen, it is very easy to replace the memory and hard drive, unlike many recent premium laptops that are glued shut with non-removable components. The back cover can be easily removed to gain access to the memory and ssd. It comes with a 128GB NVMe x2 M.2 2280 WD SN520 SSD, that can be replaced with any 2280 NVMe ssd. Be aware though that only 2 PCIe lanes are connected, so any x4 ssd will run in x2 mode, limiting the bandwidth, but it's still much faster than SATA based SSDs. There are 2 DDR4 SODIMM slots, one occupied by the 4GB stick that comes with the machine, but can be removed to install a bigger stick. The processor supports DDR4-2400 speeds. I have installed 2x8GB memory, and based on the measured memory bandwidth I can confirm that it operates in dual-channel mode. The machine also has an empty slot for a 2.5" drive, which is useful for those that need lots of cheap storage on board, but using that would reduce battery life. The processor is pretty fast, on par with Intel Core i3 netbooks, and the integrated Radeon graphics easily beats the integrated graphics in Intel chips, especially with the upgraded dual channel memory, but obviously this is not a gaming laptop. Pros: Great price, upgradable memory (32GB should work), upgradable 2280 NVMe SSD, empty 2.5" HDD slot, beautiful screen, gigabit RJ45 port, lightweight Cons: not so great battery life, no SD card reader, no USB-C port, cheap speakers, air intake at the bottom

title: Great everyday laptop.
text: I bought this Notebook elsewhere, however, I just wanted to let everyone know that this is the best budget laptop I've seen and I tested few from Lenovo, HP and Acer. Two of attached screenshots show results of graphic Geekbench test, one with 4GB second with upgraded to (with 4GB stick) 8GB RAM. Overall, the most distinguishing features have to be FHD 1080p IPS screen, decent keyboard and trackpad. Here's more detailed list: Pros: Sturdy casing, lid does not look cheap or 'economy' Hinge works well, does not wobble when open Screen is high contrast, IPS, with enough brightness for most indoor conditions. Screen is high contrast at low brightness levels which makes it less tiring when viewing at night. Screen does not show motion blur when scrolling fast. Screen viewing angles are good and brighness does not change from one corner to the other when in front of it. Screen is 1080P ! Screen is matte, non-glare. Back-light is flicker-free ( I think.. I usually can detect flicker below 240Hz ) Touchpad is large, accessible without straining you hand, fingers glide over it smoothly. Touchpad buttons are not hard to press, though would prefer if button area was not touch sensitive Keys, although with shallow travel, are not hard to press (much less springy than Lenovo 330S for example) and are easy to type with Keyboard has a backlight Numeric keypad, although cramped, it's convenient to have. Laptop fan is quiet (almost inaudible) when browsing or watching videos. Sound is ok once you get realtek drivers (otherwise it's way too quiet) Drive is fast, normally larger capacity SSD drives are fast but this 128GB is great. Battery life is fine once you tweak mobile Ryzen settings (otherwise it can be too short and varying greatly depending on task) Can add second, SATA6, SSD drive, and it supports up to 32GB of RAM in two slots (2x 16GB of DDR4 2400 or 2666) No RAM is soldered in, like on Vivobook for example. Performance is plenty for browsing, watching videos, office applications. It's very close to Intel's 8145U processor) This laptop does not have the power button right next to delete like other, smaller Acer's do. 2x2 MIMO WIFI, with good performance Cons: Windows 10S requires account in order to downgrade to Home edition. Battery life is hard to predict as it depends greatly on the task. I managed to extend it using utility from github that tweaks mobile Ryzen settings. Once tweaked, the laptop is slower, geekbench gives it a score near Intel N5000, however battery lasts 50% longer. I do like this solution as I can have chromebook performance with long battery life or Notebook with twice the speed if I don't mind ~4h battery life or when I'm plugged in. NumLock has no LED indicator. It can play games, however, if ganes are priority, I would recommend Ryzen 2500U or 3500U processor with good cooling. 3200U with Vega 3 GPU is slightly slower than Intel's UHD620 - i.e. not fast, especially because screen is 1080P. Another con for me is that charger/PSU is proprietary and not an USB-C. At least the barrel is thicker and plugs firmly, and I think it will last longer than plugs on HPs I've seen. Lastly, as I hinted under Pros, out of the box, sound output was muddled and very quiet. At 50% it was barely audible. However, after installing Realtek's audio drivers v2.82 the sound is ok (not great but not as bad as before).

title: Some simple fixes make this a solid business/light gaming laptop.
text: When I got this laptop, the F keys were automatically preset to their functions instead of simply being F keys. Normally, you have to hold "Fn" and hit an F key to use the function, but it was reversed on this machine. Also, the keyboard backlight turned itself off after 20 seconds of inactivity whether or not it was plugged in. It kind of defeats the purpose of a backlit keyboard, in my opinion, when you can't see the keys before you start typing. At any rate, both the F key and backlight issues were mostly fixed when I updated the BIOS directly from the Acer support site. I was then able to find settings for both in BIOS and disable automatic function key and backlight timeout. My only gripe is that there doesn't seem to be any way to keep the backlight on for more than 20 seconds when unplugged, no matter the power settings or BIOS configuration. Lots of Googling and worthless Acer chat support sessions later, I'm convinced there's no workaround. That issue aside, I can't really say anything else negative about this machine. At this price point, this is about as good as it gets. If you plan on doing anything other than browsing the internet and using Office, I do recommend purchasing an additional 4GB RAM stick and installing it yourself. It took me maybe 5 minutes with a YouTube tutorial video. Between that extra RAM and the stock SSD, I can run low-end games with Chrome and Skype running in the background all at once with no slowdown whatsoever. It's lightweight, the screen is decently bright, and it'll go for hours without needing a charge. If you're in the market for a light-to-medium spec laptop for everyday use, this should be your go-to.

text: First of all I want to say that a lot of the reviews and answered questions are talking about different model numbers, not the A151-43-R19L. They talk about how a sata drive can be used to add memory, which is not true. This computer does have a sata drive slot, but for some reason it can not support it. I know this because I first bought a sata drive and it didn't work. I called the hard drive manufacture and Acer. Both of which were not a lot of help and did not know most of the questions I was asking. This is an Acer Aspire 5 . There is a lot of different models of this. For example, there is an intel and an AMD version. Please make sure you know what model you have. When you search for hard drives, make sure you put the entire model and not just Acer A151. The only way to add memory that I found to work is to replace the original NVMe PCIe that the computer comes with. In order to install this you will need to reinstall windows because this hard drive will replace the one that comes with the computer. Look up Youtube videos on how to do this. It is better to not download anything to the computer like microsoft office before doing this, because you might not be able to download it again without having to purchase the download again. I used the following hard driver: Crucial P2 500GB 3D NAND NVMe PCIe M.2 SSD - CT500P2SSD8 The RAM was easy to install Also make sure you buy at the lowest price. I bought for $480 and then 3 weeks later it costed $350. Overall the quality of the computer is great. The aluminum frame and the backlit keyboard make this computer feel expensive. title: Fine little laptop. Just get out of S mode.
text: I attached a picture of the bottom popped panel popped off. There's a lot to say about a laptop. I'll try to keep it short. First of all, Windows 11 Home in S-Mode sucks. Get it out of S-mode ASAP. S-mode allows apps only from the Microsoft store, forces the use of Microsoft Edge, and requires a Microsoft account to log in. I got it out of S-Mode and the laptop is much better. It ships with 22h2 installed. I disassembled the laptop jut to see what was going on inside. 8GB of RAM that is soldered on with no option to upgrade. The M.2 slot is full size, I believe 2280, and can be replaced easily. The CMOS battery is underneath the M.2. The main charge port is reinforced by the metal in the hinge. The Wi-Fi card can be replaced. The battery is held in by 2 screws and can be replaced. The main heatsink is decently big and replaceable. The screen has decent colors. I was going to throw on my color calibrator but variable brightness is no bueno for color accuracy. It's 60Hz and uses Free-Sync. It flexes a little bit in the center if you're holding it with one arm. The surface is matte. It's not a touch screen. The keyboard is very low profile and somewhat hard to type with slightly unkempt fingernails. I clipped my nails to better use the keyboard. It has almost every key a full size keyboard does except for a few, and even an addition of 2. It does not have a lower right Function/Context and Windows key. It doesn't have Home, End, Page Up, and Page Down keys. It is missing Scroll Lock and Pause/Break Between the F12 and Print Screen keys there is a key labeled with a CROP symbol. It starts a screenshot. Similar to Windows+Shift+S hotkey. Power Button on the keyboard, top right. That's all the button discrepancies from a full size keyboard. The mouse pad is really big and has no discrete buttons. Monolithic style. It's actually pretty hard to use and feels a bit cludgy for one-handed use. The large size lends itself to 2 handed use. By default right clicking can be achieved by tapping with 2 fingers or by pushing on the lower right section. Since it doesn't have a touch screen it's a bit difficult to navigate. If the laptop isn't totally idle it's basically always spinning the fan. It's decently quiet but audible in a library. The hotspot would be right where the CPU is which happens to be on the left thigh. It's not particularly uncomfortable but may cause a sweat on hot days. It charges via the DC barrel jack OR the adjacent USB-C port. The included charger uses the DC barrel jack. The specs on the bottom say 19v @ 2.37a, which comes out to 45-ish watts. I plugged in a USB-C charge block that can put out 90W and my USB power meter read out 19.78v at 2.9a, which is just short of 60W. I then plugged in a Thunderbolt Dock that can supposedly put out 120W and my wall meter read 62W (there could be some loss). Just remember, the DC jack is reinforced. The USB-C port is NOT reinforced. Probably not a good idea to move the laptop around when charging on USB-C and having the cable fling around. The processor is Zen2. I benched it on BananaBench and got 148Mbeam/s. Doesn't mean much to the majority of people but just know that it's not a powerhouse. The GPU isn't all that powerful either but better than the average intel integrated gpu. I failed to keep it short. My b.

title: Great for what it is
text: For what this is supposed to be and for roughly $200, it's fantastic. This isn't a high performance gaming laptop (or really any kind of gaming laptop) and it would be difficult to do precise graphic design work. However, for internet access and word processing and all of your everyday computer uses, it's one of the best you can get. This runs smooth and feels very snappy due to the solid-state drive, and Windows 10 works well. Streaming movies/shows like through Netflix or YouTube works great. If you want to install programs that aren't on the Windows app store, you'll need to disable "S mode", but this is easy and quick to do. Just Google "disable S mode" and you'll find the steps easy enough. 64 Gbs is more than enough for windows, web surfing, movie streaming, and word processing. However, I wanted to store some photos and other media, so I picked up a 256Gb micro SD card and it seems to work very well. These are relatively inexpensive ($30 or so) and couldn't be easier to install - just insert into the micro SD slot until it clicks. The screen is small for a laptop, but if you've been working with only a smartphone screen for a while like I had been, it seems huge. 😂 ASUS is one of the best quality computer parts manufacturers around, so this also should last a good while. Overall, I definitely recommend this for your more basic computer needs.

The Celeron is as expected - medium speed, zero hiccups or hangups, mild exclusion from some of your fancier computing ambitions (compatibility). I bought two and installed Linux Mint on both, both run smooth, silent, and cool. No fans, an acceptable trackpad (I hate middle mouse buttons...I haven't found a way to map that thing to register as a standard left click yet..), empty SSD space, and all of the components registered with Linux Mint instantly EXCEPT the realtek wifi card. For that, you'll need to plug into a USB wifi dongle and perform a couple driver updates. So - I now have one in Mexico and one in New York, both of which I use to control CNC machinery. title: Great Interface But You Can't Do Anything With It!!!
text: This laptop gets all the points for the interface components: - Excellent sound - Crisp screen with gorgeously vivid colors - Easy-to-access quick controls like volume mixer and internet connection tab - Clean, professional-looking exterior and keyboard Past the surface, though, everything falls apart completely unless you live (and pay) your entire life online. You cannot download any type of office software AT ALL. Want to use Office? Already paid for a copy? Too bad. You have to buy a monthly subscription to use the app version of Office online! That or do all your work in Google docs. As someone who is required to use Office for work and who already paid full price for a copy, I am appalled that I got a brand new laptop that is *useless* for my needs. I am doubly annoyed because this feature/restriction wasn't noted anywhere - if I'd known I never would have gone for this. Nor can you download pretty much anything else - any information, documents, photos, etc. that you want to store you either have to keep online or you have to have an external harddrive or jump drives for. The computer also keeps resetting to its original browser 'defaults' ever time I turn it off (and it subsequently updates), even though I've gone through and changed them because the default search engines, etc. are terrible. TL/DR: If you already live your entire life online and already pay to keep all of your information, documents, etc. in cloud storage or on an external harddrive and you're a big fan of google, this will be the perfect laptop for you and you'll love it. If you actually need/want anything on the computer itself - and to avoid the pile of monthly payments that come with totally online work/storage - this laptop will do nothing for you. I just wish someone (anyone!) had told me that before I tried it.

text: This chromebook was a big upgrade from my 6 year old chromebook but in one way it felt like taking a step back. My old chromebook for the same price point had a fan and never had overheating issues unless I really pushed it. This new style of chromebook however doesn't utilize fan cooling and claims that the new processor chips are created to not require anything beyond passive cooling by temporarily dropping the chip power if things get too hot. This might work for people simply using the device as a document tool, but the world has shifted to streaming entertainment media and that is where this chromebook falls very short. While the chromebook has a 1080p screen it can only stream 1080p content for maybe 30 minutes before the chip is forced to scale down in power to help cool off. Doing this demolishes the chromebooks ability to stream content, causes lots of hitching and lagging, and makes you either turn the content down BELOW 720p to cool off or just stop streaming content altogether. This is a big deal since a lot of people are going to want to stream at the resolution the screen is capable of. Other than that the HP 14 works great.

title: Touchpad malfunctions; HP doesn't back up warranty
text: We had this chromebook for less than a year when the touchpad began malfunctioning, rendering it unusable. After exhausting all the possible fixes we could do on our own, I attempted to contact HP, as the next recommended step was to contact the manufacturer. First problem: HP stated that our one year warranty began before we purchased the product and ended prior to our one year anniversary of purchasing it. I filled out the form to dispute the warranty, but haven't received confirmation of the resolution as of 17 days later. There is no where on their website to check the status of the inquiry, which leads to my second problem: HP does not provide any way to talk to a person when you need customer service. None. They have an AI chat, which did not have my issues in its script. It can forward you to the online "support community", but nowhere can you interact with a human to resolve your problem. It's just some general forums with no active HP personnel interaction, at least as far as I experienced. To sum up: HP either uses inaccurate record keeping or possibly less complimentary means, resulting in their stance that they do not have to stand by their warranties, and they have no interest in providing a positive (or even useful) customer service experience. If a product is defective, you are out of luck. We are now boycotting HP products. I bought a mouse at my local store, in the hopes that it would bypass the touchpad. It seems to be working adequately now, but we have to limit where we use the laptop, as we must accommodate a spot for the mouse off to the side. We are very disappointed in this product.

text: ****UPDATE 4 - 7/19/21 - Mainboard died and cost to repair is above purchasing new. Unit was out of warranty, but I purchased with a chase VISA card which extended the warranty another year. After submitting some documentation they reimbursed for cost of new and I re-purchased the laptop. Maybe I'm a glutton for punishment, but I really like the laptop when it is working. Dropped another star for poor quality control or using cheap mainboard components. ***UPDATE 3 - 12/2/20 - Have had several issues recently and wanted to pass along how I resolved them. Issue #1 was trying to boot up the computer after 12 hours of sleep and being unable to get the computer to turn on at all. Didn't matter if it was plugged in or not. The battery was fully charged. I tried holding the power button. No go, laptop was dead. As a final attempt before sending it in for service, I pulled off the bottom cover of the laptop and disconnected the battery cable for several minutes. I plugged it back in, pressed the power button, and the laptop booted normally. Everything worked fine after that and I haven't had the issue since. Issue #2 was noticing the laptop was no longer charging when connected to the USB-C charger. Even the charging LED wouldn't come on. The fix was to shut down the computer completely, then hold the power button for 20-40 seconds. The charge light came on and the laptop started charging again. **UPDATE 2 - 7/2/20 - Resolved an audio stuttering issue by turning off Dolby Audio processing in the Dolby app.** *UPDATE - 6/10/20 - Dropping a star. Sent original back due to crashing issues when waking from sleep. Wifi also dropped occasionally and had trouble reconnecting after sleep. New unit seems to work fine. Also replaced wireless card with Intel AX200 (need torx T5 bit to remove bottom panel). Much faster and no dropped connections. Still really like the laptop (and Amazon's return policy).* Original Review: Overall usability – Everything about the laptop feels well-built and like it should cost hundreds more. Incredibly fast processor, especially given the 15W TDP. The AMD Ryzen 4000 series processors (7nm Zen 2) have really improved the thermals and efficiency to the same level as Intel (or better). Between the 6 core processor and the PCIe NVMe SSD the laptop flies. Nothing I’ve thrown at it has been able to slow it down or make it stutter. Benchmarks comparable to my HP desktop with i7-7700 (if in best performance mode while plugged in). Applications open instantly in most cases. Comes out of short-term sleep instantly. Nice webcam privacy cover. Fingerprint reader is best I’ve used in terms of accuracy and speed. Fans are quiet under normal loads and a low non-annoying whirring when the GPU/CPU is taxed. Exterior – Very light weight (but not cheap feeling) and nice sturdy build. Feels like it will hold up well. Keyboard back-light adjustable. Plenty of ports. Hinges also feel built to last. Touchscreen – Sensitive and good feel (though I prefer matte to glossy). Works well with included pen. Bloatware – Almost none (uninstalled Skype). Speakers – Above average for price range. Not especially tinny sounding like cheaper laptops. Don’t expect bass though. The included Dolby equalizer software can help improve the sound if you don’t mind experimenting. Side-mounted front-facing speakers are well placed. Screen – Brightness OK for indoor use, but I plan to run it at 90% brightness even on battery because anything less is too dim. Colors are bright. No noticeable back light bleed. Battery life – Above average for price range. Really quite impressive. Could easily last half to three-quarters of the stated 10 hours depending on the conditions (clearly not doing anything processor or graphics intensive for the duration, but web browsing, office work, or video viewing). Wireless/Bluetooth – Some occasional random disconnects and trouble connecting after sleep, likely due to Realtek wireless card. Average speeds on my 5GHz home network. Keyboard/Trackpad – High quality feel. You can tell when you’ve hit a key unlike cheaper laptops. Miss the numpad, but knew it didn’t have one before I ordered. Trackpad not over-sensitive or unresponsive. Good balance, but still prefer a mouse. Graphics/Gaming – Played Two-Point Hospital on Steam at 1080p very high graphics setting. Not very graphics intensive or an FPS, but the game is newer and frame-rate didn’t drop below 30 in game. Game load times are ridiculously fast. Downsides – Mediocre webcam. Soldered RAM (not a big deal w/16 GB, but if it goes bad it is a big problem). Screen may not be bright enough for outdoor use and the glossy coating leads to reflections/glare when viewing from an angle. Wireless card not great. Stories of poor tech support (though, admittedly I’ve never interacted with them). **Don’t forget to create your USB backup drive from the Lenovo website for crashes/re-installs. title: Amazing product, a lot of misinformation from Lenovo Rep on Amazon
text: Before I tell you about how good the product is, I have to give feedback on the Lenovo Rep(s). Before the product was available, I asked if the laptop had dual channel and or single channel memory. This is easily the most important specification in terms of performance for AMD laptops because the integrated graphics are very powerful, but you essentially lose half of the igpu performance with single channel memory. The rep told me (and subsequently another person) that the laptop has single channel memory. This is incorrect. I looked up the model number of the laptop on Geekbench and it clearly stated that it is dual channel. I received my laptop and checked with CPUZ, it also says dual channel. Now some people may say "well what are you complaining for? You're mad because your laptop is better than they said it was?" No, I'm upset because the rep's job is to give correct information to consumers so that they can make good purchasing decisions. Incorrect information causes lost sales and it makes both AMD and Lenovo look incompetent. If you look through all of the questions on the Amazon product page, you will see a few other instances of incorrect information. Just to be clear, this is a very good product in my opinion. It comes with a usb-c charger, a stylus, a mechanical shutter for the webcam, a ten keyless led keyboard. The screen is decent, obviously not something you would use for professional graphic design but it is still very good for the average user. The build quality is great, very solid. The 2 in 1 functionality is very cool in combination with the stylus. The performance is in a completely different league from anything else in this price range. AMD's new Ryzen 4000 cpu's are insane. Benchmarked next to my 2500U, this 4500U is about 90% faster in terms of cpu performance. The igpu is up to 50% faster than the Vega 8 graphics in my 2500U. This laptop is ideal for a mixture of office work, consuming media, and light gaming. If you want something to play LoL, Dota, Rocket League, CSGO, etc or random indie games on Steam, then this laptop can do that. For $600 there is nothing you can get from Intel that can match this performance without having a discrete Nvidia gpu. The only thing I dislike is that the SSD is 256GB, but I have a 512GB mini usb that I can use for media so it's fine. My first impressions: highly recommend... but get your stuff together, Lenovo Rep, whoever you are.

title: Pen doesn't work with Windows 11
text: Updating my review and taking away a couple stars. I'll leave the original review below. I recently installed Windows 11 and everything works well EXCEPT for the pen. The included pen was one of the main reasons I purchased this laptop. I've tried uninstalling and reinstalling the drivers, and I have not been able to get the pen to work again. I'm now trying to find out if I can revert back to Windows 10 to be able to use my pen again. My Lenovo Flex 5 14" 2-in-1 laptop arrived yesterday, so I've only just begun using it, but I have a lot of good things to say about it already. The build quality is impressive, which I'm pleasantly surprised about. I was a little concerned about it being that it's all plastic, but it feels very premium. My last laptop was a Lenovo U430 touch, which had a metal case. But that one had some quality control issues as the top and bottom parts of the case didn't line up well and there were some sharp edges. Even though this one is plastic, it looks and feels much nicer than my older Lenovo. There is a little flex in the screen and in the lower part of the chassis, but the keyboard has very little flex and the hinges feel very sturdy. Another thing I was concerned about was the display. I've read/seen some reviews stating that the screen isn't bright enough and that the colors weren't great, but I think this display will get the job done for me. It will mostly be used in the office on my desk, so I may connect it to an external monitor for more "real estate," but the colors and brightness don't appear to be an issue for indoor use. Sitting in my well-lit office right now with all the windows open, the display is bright enough, although I do need to have it on max. I definitely wouldn't recommend this for regular outdoor use, but it should be fine for indoor use. The surface of the screen is a little "sticky" feeling when using touch input. My older Lenovo felt more "glassy" and my fingers glide on the screen more like they do on my smartphone. This isn't a huge deal to me as I don't plan to use touch input all the time. When I do, I'm mostly tapping. It's only the swiping and dragging actions that feel a little strange. Even though the laptop overall is very compact, thin, and light, it is a little unwieldly in tablet mode, so I don't see myself using it as a tablet for long periods of time. My iPad is still a much more pleasant experience for that. The Lenovo pen works well and it's great that it was included with the laptop. I can see that being very useful. It's not as nice as the Apple pencil, so I probably wouldn't use it much for writing or drawing, but it will be handy for marking up documents. The last thing I was concerned about was the wifi connection, which I have heard negative comments about. So far the wifi hasn't been a major problem, but I have noticed a few hiccups. I was streaming music from Google Play Music last night, and there were several times where the music stuttered. I'm not sure if that's an issue with the sound card driver or the wifi card. Hopefully it will be corrected with a driver or firmware update in the future. At any rate, it's a minor annoyance that I can live with. If it doesn't get fixed, I'll probably spend $20 and replace the Realtek wifi card with a superior Intel card, since that component is user replaceable (although it would probably void my 1 year warranty). The computer seems to be plenty powerful, thanks to the Ryzen 4500u, the solid state drive, and the 16gb of memory. The fan keeps the laptop comfortably cool, and it's not overly loud. I have a desktop with a Ryzen 5 1600 and I love it, so I intentionally sought out a laptop with the latest generation of mobile Ryzen processors. After comparing this Lenovo to available models from Acer, Dell, and HP, this seemed to have the best set of features for the price. This laptop should do everything I need it to do, and then some. I have not tested the built-in camera or microphone yet, but the speakers sound very nice. Not really much bass, but the sound is better than I expected it to be. The finger print reader is very nice and works as well as the finger print reader on my smartphone—very accurate and quick. This laptop checks all the right boxes for me, and I can tell it's going to be a pleasure to use. I agree with many of the reviews that I've seen/read. This laptop will be great for office work, students, and casual gamers. This is probably not the laptop to get for creative professionals or those who plan to work outside. They will need something with a brighter screen with more accurate colors. Overall, I'm a happy repeat customer with Lenovo and I'm very pleased with this laptop so far.

title: great machine for the price, with several issues, not totally working out of the box
text: This is a major upgrade for me from my 5 year old surface tablet. Handles productivity tasks with blazing fast speed, doesn't get overwhelmed by the sea of browser tabs I need to do my job. Finger print reader works great, touch screen and pen is responsive, the hinge is sturdy without being stiff, trackpad is sensitive, keyboard is comfortable, speakers are great, average battery life, getting around 7 hours of work off a full charge, but could definitely go longer with lower screen brightness and less intense usage. Some flaws: - my built in webcam routinely blinks out: I thought this was a software thing and checked everything from privacy settings, to device manager and drivers, to lenovo's software settings. Eventually, it started working again but then would randomly blink off, and disappear from device manager when it did so. I figured out that rotating the laptop or changing the angle of the screen could sometimes get it back on, which makes me think it's a hardware issue and the webcame is not securely attached. even when it is working, it's pretty low res. - integrated microphone doesn't record any sound: i guess this isn't the biggest deal since i always deal with calls over headphone, but annoying. registers in device manager, but does not record any sound. all software settings, including privacy, was explored. - laptop gets very hot when entering sleep mode, unusable: the fan and heat ramp up when the laptop goes into sleep mode, much more warm than when I'm using it normally, making it dangerous to leave the laptop inside a case when in sleep mode. i had to disable sleep mode when not plugged in to prevent overheating and battery drain. i have it set that lid closing puts the laptop into hibernation, which isn't the worse thing, just takes an extra 2-3 seconds to wake the computer up. - usb ports kinda stiff: had to really push to get accessories seated into the ports, was mildly worried of damaging it. I think maybe it's starting to loosen up slightly. All in all, the things that don't work are huge concerns, and I can work around it, but they are annoying with this being a new laptop. Getting service with Lenovo is a pain in the ass. They respond irregularly to forum posts about technical issues, don't send you a confirmation about your service ticket, call you randomly without leaving a message for call back, tell you to schedule a call back time when your produce is marked as being ineligible for scheduled call backs, and to top it off, when I did call and started speaking to a rep, the call got dropped, and I saw no attempt at calling back. Might update this if they ever get back to me. UPDATE: Amazon agreed to send me a replacement, and all the previous issues I mentioned, the camera, the mic, the overheating issue, are all resolved in the replacement unit. BUT, it has different issues. The first is one that just baffles me (and is vaguely concerning) which is it weighs approximately 0.5 ounces less than the first one I got. It's supposed to be the same model so I can't imagine what would account for the weight difference. I mean, I prefer the lighter weight but...what??? Also, the keyboard build quality appears to be different, although this issue is a slight improvement in that the keys feel a bit springier, although it's also audibly more clacky too. Another build difference, the hinge on the first unit felt much smoother and sturdier, while the replacement unit has certain parts of its range where it feels looser or stiffer. Lastly, the colors/brightness will randomly get washed out with the replacement unit, especially when waking from sleep. It doesn't render the display unusable at all, it's just quite noticeable, and annoys me. The colors on the first unit appear richer and with better contrast. And most significantly, the battery at full charge seems to only last 4-5 hours as opposed to the 8-9 hours I was getting with the first one I received. Again for $600, I'm not expecting anything too remarkable, and the new unit is fine and performs just as well as the first one from a processing and productivity standpoint. It's fast, and can handle a slew of browser tabs, and even runs games fine, albeit older ones, and with some graphics settings turned down. With a pen and touchscreen, a 360 hinge, 16gb of ram, and really good built-in speakers, it offers a killer deal and is everything I could want in an affordable laptop for work. I'll just deal with the quirks with this replacement model and keep a close watch on it while it's covered under warranty. UPDATE 2: I sent the last one back due to its suspected refurbished status and the new one I received has all the build quality issues resolved. The keyboard is as quiet as the first one, and the hinge feels far more secure. However, I'm still finding the battery is lasting only around 5 hours, so I'm not sure what's going on, if they perhaps changed the battery to lighten the weight of the machine. It is the same weight as the 2nd unit I received.

title: Great Specs, Good Price.
text: Edit 12/13/20: Linux (EndeavourOS, Garuda) runs fine with latest kernels (5.8+) and the latest BIOS updates. SSD upgrade is easy, but finding a good external nvme enclosure for SSD cloning is not. Battery life is quite good. Fan noise can be a bit loud if maxing out the 6 CPU cores but the laptop is usually silent just browsing the internet. Excellent value, decent performance - no problems so far in 5 months Original: This laptop just hit the market recently. All the basic hardware functions work, but little things still need to be ironed out. The touchpad under Windows is quite erratic. The touch pressure required varies from light to heavy just to be sensed. Other times, touches are ignored up to several seconds. I don't see this hesitance when running linux. But under linux, the screen brightness control won't dim below 70%. So at night the laptop screen can be a little too bright. Also the touchscreen doesn't work with all linux distros (yet) but it works well with windows. I'd expect full linux support with a newer kernel within the next couple of months. Linux, kernel 5.7 already has a lot of support. I won't be using windows enough to notice when its touchpad driver gets fixed. Performance: A large compile takes just under 14 minutes on my i5-6400 desktop with 7200RPM hard disk. The same compile on the Flex takes just over 7 minutes. Not quite twice as fast, but it's about what I was hoping for. While compiling, the fan came on full (it is multi-speed), but it is respectably quiet compared to my old laptop. I highly recommend this laptop at this price point with the caveat that such a new processor will need some OS/BIOS updates to be at its best. But I'm actually very happy with the Flex5 so far. I gained almost an inch of screen size over my old 13" laptop, but both laptops are about the same size. The keyboard has real keys with short travel and good backlighting. For linux, key backlighting is not supported with kernels older than 5.7. If I was going to improve this laptop, I'd find room for one more USB port and double the SSD size. 256GB is good for a single OS system, but it's a little cramped for my needs. The battery charger plugs into the USB-C port, even though there is a power jack. An alternate charger did solve my USB port shortage. At the Lenovo site, the same model costs more, for half the RAM and without the active pen. This is a great bundle as of July '20..

text: I recently bought this laptop (a week ago) and it is truly a dream! Editing pictures on Photo shop and Affinity Photo has been an absolute breeze! title: Great laptop, but its the little things
text: So purchased this laptop as I sold the previous gen of this exact laptop (AMD 3500u). To my sister for her at home college classes. So I have some background using these series of Lenovo laptop. The over all build fit and finish is much better then the previous gen, its actually smaller, depth and with, yet only a HAIR bit thicker. The case is sturdy and the hinges are tight! So the display stays at the angle you desire. The plastic is a bit more 'plasticy' feeling then the previous gen. Which had the 'softer' feel to it. The power.... the R5 3500u, that I had been using was a powerhouse already, but I honestly was not expecting THIS much of a improvement with the 4500u. Games such as WoW classic and LoL, near high settings at native 1080p res, a good soild 40-60fps with V-sync on. I think we are seeing the start of dedicated graphics cards in laptops on the way out, if AMD keeps this up. The 256gb NVME SSD is quite fast, not as fast as a Samsung EVO/PRO drives, but still around the 2000 Read / 1200 Write MBs area so its quite snappy. 16gb Dual channel DDR4 is a welcome over the 12gb of the previous gen. The screen.. well its a screen, its IPS, its a touch screen. The brightness of the screen is best suited for darker environments as other have stated. Its kinda of the weakest point of this laptop if your looking for something that can be used outside a lot. The included stylus is very nice and quite fun to play with even if your not into the graphic use side of it. I will recommend a plastic style screen protector, as the stylus tip kinda 'catches'' on the glass of the display and makes a bit harder to work with fine movements, a plastic protector eliminated this issue. Battery, the life of this battery is stunning. Full brightness, I was able to pull 4+ hours of streaming tv while away from the outlet. It comes with a USB-C charger, but it can still use the previous gen power-block as it has the normal style charging port. This was handy in my case as I had bought two other power bricks to keep at my summer and work locations, so no need to buy more USB-C chargers. Ports and Misc. USB-C, HDMI, 2 x USB 3.0 and SD slot. Pretty much run of the mill array of input/output for ports. I would like to see just a mini-SD slot instead of a full SD slot. Would make for adding extra space to the limited 256gb with out having to upgrade the entire drive. Nitpicks, I will say there is a few things that disappoint me from my previous one, its all minor things thankfully. 1. So far...the back-light on keyboard does NOT stay on all the time, only when using it. This CAN be fixed via software update, so hoping Lenovo reads this and fixes it. :) 2. No hot keys for turning the touch pad/touch screen, on/off. Kinda hand if you want to eliminate mouse movements when your typing etc 3. Speakers are NOT as loud as the previous gen, despite them being forward facing now. Overall you can NOT beat this laptop for the power and price you pay for it. If your looking for something that will last a few years for power wise and not in to heavy gaming, this should be in your consideration for purchase. I'm glad I still upgrade from the 3500u, even if I did not own it for a full year, the power is amazing!

title: Impressive Laptop. Do not recommend.
text: The screen is not great, but I did my research and expected it. Overall I found the speed and responsiveness of the laptop to be impressive, thanks to the 4500U processor. If the third time was a charm this probably would have received a review of four stars rounded up from 3.75 Returning this laptop has been a a pain and fraught with delays. Initially I was told it would take 3-5 days to receive a refund. Then I was told 1 week, then 2 weeks. It took 4 weeks. title: DO NOT BUY: Absolute trash support
text: Far and away the worst support of any PC manufacturer I've ever seen. Lenovo is downright shady. Trying to Google it brings up the "Active Pen 2," which looks completely different. So right out the door, basic things about this tablet make absolutely 0 sense to the consumer. The pen also desyncs constantly. The pen will stop controlling the cursor, but the buttons still work. Sometimes using the secondary buttons fixes it, other times it doesn't. I frequently find myself stabbing at the screen because it just doesn't respond to any other action. Let's say you're ready to look for support for this pen instead of stabbing at the screen! Good luck, because every customer support response is a garbled, incoherent mess that has virtually nothing to do with what you're searching for. Look no further than the Q&A section on this listing--Lenovo's own representatives say no pen comes with this tablet, which is FALSE. The support for this product is a complete joke. I tried to go to live chat for support, and they say they aren't open and to "check the hours." Go back to the support page, the hours aren't listed anywhere. Most likely it'd be some clueless Engrishy stooge anyway. Product is a complete waste of your time and money. Update: I contacted Lenovo support via chat, and the rep literally could not tell me anything about this pen. Instead they sent me a replacement (?!) which naturally still desyncs because it is flawed by design. Do not buy this laptop if you're serious about your pen use. Update 12/28/20: Laptop shorted out and smells like burnt copper around the left hinge, holding the power button causes the power lights to strobe. No expectation they're going to fix it. Stay away. title: Solid performance for the price
text: I got this for work to replace an old Surface Pro 2 with the dual core I3, 4 gigs of ram and 64 gigs of storage. As Chrome and various websites consume more and more ram these days it was starting to struggle with all the tabs I keep open. Out of the box it boots up fine, minimal bloatware and not bad specs for the built in NVME drive. The 16 gigs of ram fixed all my browser issues and the screen is decent but not great, definitely a step down from the Surface screen. Upside is the back is removed relatively easy provided you have the right set of drivers. I swapped the drive to a Samsung EVO 960, for a significant performance increase and swapped the wifi card for an Intel AX200 card. Huge increase in both versus the native devices. Installed a clean install of Windows 10 and AMD's drivers and it's good to go. Anyone experiencing overheating, just be careful not to smother the vents on the bottom of the case, it could probably use slightly taller feet. Sitting it flat on a bed or something similar though and it will struggle to pull air in. I haven't had the issue but I'm mindful of the vents. A side vent would have been a better design for users not paying attention to the vents.

title: Excellent Value. With some drawbacks
text: I am extremely happy with my purchase. I needed a budget laptop that could keep up with my workloads, and this laptop delivers excellent performance. The only downside is the 256GB ssd, but it was very easy to upgrade to a 2280 1Tb ssd, you just take off the back panel and it's right there. As for some negatives. The only USB 3.0 port is the USB C charging port. However, there is a dedicated power port on the laptop. I ended up buying a $25 charger that fits it so I could use the USB C port and have it plugged in at the same time. The plastic is a bit cheap and scratches easily, which I expected for this price range. But if you need a rugged laptop this may not be the one for you. The pen is also pretty flimsy, and $60 to replace. I broke the tip almost immediately. Admittedly, it was my fault, because I did not store it securely in my bag. Highly recommend you get a case for the pen. Also, Linux users be aware, getting the AMD graphics drivers functioning was a pain. And I still have some glitches, like if I lower the screen brightness more than half it just shuts off the backlight. This is not really the laptops fault, it just comes with the territory of using Linux on brand new hardware. All in all, excellent value for money. Very happy with my purchase.

title: Fan Noise
text: I've returned this laptop and kept the HP ENNY version with same hardware configuration. Lenovo should've put 2 fans or at least have more openings for air flow to this device. 4500u is a great APU as it delivers high performance with low energy consumption. I was looking for silent operation with this. However, this laptop is always loud with the fan even if you just run 2 chrome tabs. HP ENVY version with same 4500u and such has 2 fans and more grills. I rarely hear any fan noise even in some games. I think that chassis is also being metal is helping compared to this plastic one. Anyway, if you don't care about fan noise and some possible throttling, this device is a good option. Should be future-proof for office/school work and some casual gaming for next 5 years with the 4th gen Ryzen and 16gb ram.

title: This computer is amazing
text: I rarely write review products for items because I feel like they do not require them. This 2 in 1 is different because I genuinely enjoy using this computer. I will break this down into things, and I will mention both pros and cons. KEYBOARD Pros: It is incredibly tactile and easy to type on, it is clicky and it lights up so, it's easy to see what you're typing in less than ideal conditions. Overall, it is a major pro of the Flex 5. Cons: no number pad and no full-size arrow keys SCREEN Pros: It is a good size and the bezels are minimal. It's a touchscreen and it comes with a pen that's pressure-sensitive. Cons: More technical reviews say that it is not quite as color accurate but in reality... It is satisfactory for most people. HARDWARE: Pros: Incredibly portable 2 in 1, so it can act like a regular laptop and a windows tablet. It is able to charge through both the traditional Lenovo barrel connector and the USB C port. It also has other ports that include USB 3.0 ports, HDMI port Cons: Primarily plastic build and no thunderbolt. 256 GB SSD may not be enough for some people, but it is expandable! PROCESSOR: Pros: REALLY good.... Like REEAAALLLLYYYYY good. This thing is plenty fast for most things! 16 GB DDR4 ram, not low power RAM, so that means that it is plenty fast for loading items already in the memory. It is faster than most comparable 10th gen Intel core i5 and i7 processors. Cons: no dedicated GPU, so not really what you would consider a gaming laptop. That is ok for most people! RAM is not upgradeable, it does not have Wifi 6, but neither of those is a deal-breaker. OVERALL: For $700, it's a good deal! For $600, it's a steal! It is such a good laptop for most people that I would recommend to someone who needs a portable and powerful 2 in 1. That is why I'm making this review!

title: Cheapest 4500U+ AMD Laptop... But....
text: The laptop is really poorly constructed. Cheap plastic, hinges that allow the screen to close by itself if it's at any angle at all. It's annoying to use unless your sitting upright or at a desk. You won't be able to use it while laying in bed etc. The processing power is pretty good for such a small laptop, and battery life is decent. The touchscreen is pretty good (but I don't use it for graphic design purposes). Speakers are terrible. Tinny sound and cheaply made. They are decently loud. The screen is awful brightness wise, and also color clarity. You won't be able to use this outside or in bright rooms. It's also small. You might think you only need 14 inches, but going from this computer to a 16 inch macbook there is a clear difference. The touchpad is awful as well. It is cheap plastic and there is a large gap between the chassis and the touchpad. This means you can easily get crumbs, hair (I have 3 pets) in the crevice causing the touchpad to malfunction. Basically, if your sole concern is the maximum amount of processing power for the least money this is your computer. If you care about anything else, this laptop is pretty terrible. Maybe at this price point bad build quality is a given but $600 is still a lot of money. Had multiple software related issues and tech support has not been helpful.

title: Stay Away!
text: I bought this laptop back in August of 2020 and by the end of October 2020, it was a brick. Would not turn on. Nearly two months for repairs after repeated calls and emails asking when I would get my laptop back. This was certainly not an isolated incident. Just check some Lenovo forums and you'll see that thousands of people had their laptops in for service for MONTHS recently. Of course, when I got my laptop back, my hard drive was wiped and I had to reinstall everything I use for work. Not pleasant but I was just happy to have a working laptop back. A few weeks later, however, and now my touchscreen doesn't work at all. The best solution Lenovo can offer? Do a complete system reset which means wiping the hard drive again and then hoping that resolves the issue. Before this laptop, I had a Lenovo Yoga 2 Pro for several years and it worked beautifully until the hinge went bad and I wasn't even mad about that because it lasted for 5 years. I had nothing but good things to say about Lenovo but this laptop is garbage and I will certainly never buy another Lenovo product again.

title: Pretty good laptop that is also a tablet.
text: This laptop is a fine laptop at the price under $600. Mostly good because of its utility as a two-in-one. The keyboard is more mushy than a 13" Macbook Air 2020 M1 -- which is not so good, but it is useable since dealing with a 14" class computer body. And of course, this is the 4500u Ryzen 5. So, this review has a timeframe of usefulness -- for if one is buying a 4500u when other competitors have some fancier better, then, thing such should be considered on whether a given price is good. Using as a tablet -- this Windows is the best. But, windows has a poor font experience. Reading on this is good enough -- though the lack of a bright screen is annoying. 3.) Most reasonable user interface goes to Pop!_OS though not as glitch free as MacOS. (MacOS M1 has bugs and fails to have a good way of install GNU/Emacs.) 4.) Best for programming and text editing -- Pop!_OS. 5.) Best as a laptop -- Mac Air 2020 M1. 6.) Best trackpad -- Mac Air 2020 M1, though I'd think System76 has some better track pads than what I've experience with Pop!_OS nowadays. More cons than pros, but it is really the question of price. Pros: * Gaming is OK. * Windows Subsystem for Linux Works Well making the computer more useable for those who think with pipes. * Sufficient RAM for most daily tasks. * Most days the CPU is snappy. * The ability to use the computer also as a tablet is a huge reason to buy this computer -- especially for reading technical books with graphs. * Microsoft Whiteboard is a program that works well for productivity on this computer with the Active Pen. But, even so, the Intel version may be what you want for a cooler laptop. It is your decision. * Good fingerprint reader. * Takes advantage of new function key layouts for Microsoft Windows. * Physical camera shutter, potentially for more privacy. * Keyboard may be lit with the Fn-Space. A few white-light levels. Cons: * Bloatware -- Anti-virus trail with insulting text promoting Fear Uncertainty and Doubt over just using the Anti-virus that comes with Windows 10. Just uninstall the McCaffery bloat. * Adware -- Lenovo promotes buying more of their products in Windows Notifications and Toasts. Crap move Lenovo. * Keyboard keys reflect CFL lights in such a way that they are hard to read at night -- making programs that allow one to spell check a word with CTRL-. very difficult to use (Typical Spell checker in Microsoft Visual Studio Code.) * Arrow keys have a poor design for editing text -- page up and page down are on the minuscule up and down arrow keys. * Oddly had to reset my pin for no reason * Buggy transitions to tablet mode -- if done when not logged in sometimes doesn't register the change. * Active pen takes up both USB type A ports. * Power cord takes up the other, and only, USB, type C, port. * Has an additional barrel jack Power inlet, but no way to use it. * Can run warm, but tolerable. Even when doing not much more than typing or reading a Kindle Cloud reader based book. * Sound is OK-ish. * Battery life is ho-hum. * Computer doesn't actually ever turn off when asking it to. Instead, it will eat up battery in hibernate mode. * "Fn" key needs to be processed to enable keys such as F1, F2, F3, F4, &etc. This is odd since now to close a program it is Fn-Alt-F4 which is bad ergonomics. Though one can lock the function key mode with Fn-ESC as a toggle not unlike the Caps Lock -- So, perhaps more of a Ah-ha. * Yucky feel of the keys and trackpad -- the keys have an odd friction, but are OK. title: Very well balanced performance for the price
text: This laptop has A LOT going for it at under $600. It's not a no compromise unit like you'd expect for double the price, but this unit has a lot to like. First the things I like about this unit: It comes with 16 GB of DDR4 memory, while other laptops in the price range are still trying to get away with the same amount of memory that came in mid range laptops 10 years ago. The screen is IPS and touch enabled. It's not a very bright screen and the color gamut is on the small side, but it's reasonably well calibrated out of the box and is bright enough for indoor use. It comes with a stylus. I don't know how much use anyone will get out of it, but it's in the box for those that want to do some drawing on the touch interface. The CPU is very good. In this price range you'll usually get one of the older gen CPUs or a very slow intel i5. The 4500u in this unit has 6 full cores and they're fast and efficient. It comes with nvme storage. It's not uncommon in the sub $600 range to still find a HDD instead of an SDD. The SDD in this isn't cutting edge, or anything, but when put together with the rest of the package it helps support the overall balanced good performance of this unit. Now for the things I didn't like about this unit: The charger it comes with plugs into the USB C port. I'm not sure why Lenovo is doing this since the unit also has a barrel plug. Just include a barrel plug charger so that people can have the USB C port open for peripheral use while the charger is plugged in. This is probably the most annoying thing about this laptop. The laptop also doesn't have any optical drive. It's becoming standard and expected that units don't have optical drives anymore, and it probably contributes to keeping the size and weight down on the unit, but I'm someone that still likes the idea of getting an optical drive in a laptop. This laptop doesn't have an ethernet port. This is probably the second most annoying part after the USB C charger, since the base of the unit is thick enough to have an ethernet port. I picked up a $12 tp-link USB 3 to ethernet adapter to go with the unit, but it probably would have added less than $5 to the bill of materials cost for this unit to sell it with an ethernet port built in. With the pros and cons noted, I'll add that the unit has a pretty solid feel for being housed in plastic, and is very snappy in use. The keyboard is decent, and the overall usability of the unit is very good. For the price I'd say the level of hardware included makes it a good value that probably only lags behind laptops costing twice as much in very minor ways for most users.

title: Decent gaming and great quality at a crazy low price
text: It’s hard to find a decent gaming laptop in the price range, so I was a little skeptical about this laptop. And while it has a few quirks, I think it’s a good value and a great choice for a “kids first laptop.” The main things keeping the price down are the CPU and the SSD drive size. The small SSD size is a gaming limiter, but that’s an easy and cheap upgrade for later (the MB has a SATA slot and an M2 slot so you can add a second drive pretty easily or have your local tech shop do it). The CPU in my model is a solid Ryzen R5-3550H which compares well with newer Intel i5 CPUs. It has 4 dual threaded cores for a total of 8 virtual cores. It clocks up to 3.7GHz with a reasonable 4MB cache. It’s not the most powerful CPU but delivers solid performances on enough threads to make it good for gaming. It’s also reasonable cool (TDP 35W). The CPU comes with on-die Vega 8 graphics (which are mediocre) but that doesn’t really matter because there is a discrete GeForce GTX 1650 Graphics CPU. That’s the entry level Turing core GPU, and doesn’t include ray tracing or tensor cores (found in the RTX 2000 line), but it still performs better than the older Pascal cores. This CPU will generally outperform the GTX 1050 Ti. That’s not going to break any gaming records but they are going to get good frame rates on most any game. And if you look at “middle school staples” like Fortnite you can get playable frame rates with Ultra settings. The light up keyboard may annoy anyone under 18 years of age, but they’ll love it. The build quality seems really good. I mean really really good for this price range. I actually think this will stand up well to kid use. Still, it’s a $699 gaming laptop. It’s best if this isn’t subjected to too much abuse. There’s only so much you can do in this price range. Best of all: lots of beautiful full size ports. I hate “ultra-book” form factors with a few non-standard port sizes. This is made so you can hook stuff up without needing that adapter you lost. Bless them. I’m still a little skeptical that a $699 gaming laptop doesn’t suck, but so far this has proven me wrong. Most importantly my middle-age son loves it and it’s running his favorite games with no troubles. I don’t normally go for AMD, but they are making solid CPU s these days and it’s helping keep the cost down on this laptop. If you are on a budget I can’t think of a better gaming laptop in this price range. Yes you can easily spend 1K more, and if you are an uber gamer, that’s what you should do. If you are a parent looking to something that won’t break the bank and fall apart day one, this is a good choice.

title: All it takes is a little problem to make a laptop a pain to use! Update - unusable touchpad
text: UPDATE [Feb 2 2020]: Asus serviced my laptop in response to the touchpad issue that persisted through online troubleshooting. The turnaround time was acceptable, and their communication through the process was very good. Unfortunately, the touchpad issue persists. I have now found several threads online about this issue, and it appears to be a design problem. My suspicion (shared by some online) is that it is caused by radio frequency interference. Apparently the touchpad is susceptible to interference and ASUS does not shield the touchpad as many other manufacturers do. The laptop still performs well and is fine in all other aspects. If you use an external pointing device as many do, you will like this laptop, but be aware that I have done everything I can do to get this fixed, and in the end the touchpad is not usable for me. Oh, where to start with this one!? So disappointed... but this isn't a bad laptop. I have used other gaming laptops in the past, and this one stacks up well, and has it quirks like they all do. The good things include the keyboard, lighting, screen, weight, cooling and overall feel. The bad things mainly concern the keyboard, cooling, and the touchpad. The indifferent thing is the performance. I am not going to benchmark this or describe the performance in this review. It has an AMD Ryzen 5 3550H CPU and GTX 1650 GPU. You can find out if those will play the games you want using the Internet. I am happy with the performance of this laptop, and I feel as thought I had reasonable expectations based on the hardware. The memory and storage have been sufficient. It is always good to have an SSD. I have used other laptops with HDDs and hybrid SSD/HDDs, and while the additional storage is kind of appealing, the speed of an SSD during both gaming and simple everyday use is preferable. The screen looks great, but I can't say that I notice the higher refresh rate - I don't think most of the games I've played are able to get much beyond 60fps on this laptop. This is a tough laptop (literally, the product line is called TUF). Have you ever dropped a playmobile toy? They are made of plastic, and they bend or come apart if you drop them, but the plastic never breaks. That's what this laptop feels like. It is very plastic, but built in a way that I would believe it would survive a fall. I feel comfortable carrying it around, would put it into a backpack and not worry about it very much. It is not touch by being solidly built and heavy, but by being light and sort of flexible in a plastic kind of way. I have not dropped it, though. While it is definitely an entry level laptop, it does have the same lighting system for the keyboard as more expensive ASUS laptops. The lighting is well done, the backlight is useful in the dark, and it looks cool. The only complaint I have is that the power button is visible from the front/top and has a single red LED that clashes with the keyboard lighting. There are two other white indicator LEDs on the front/top that don't seem to clash as badly. Maybe I should just set the keyboard to red all the time? The cooling is a mixed bag. If you have not used a gaming laptop, get ready for a noisy experience. No gaming laptop is silent when playing games. Like others I have used, this laptop is silent or very quiet when the fan is not running, and gets very loud under full load. I have noticed that this laptop seems to be at low-level load more frequently than others I have used. That means there is low-level fan noise more frequently. Also from time to time while doing things like simply browsing the Internet, the fans will kick in and get noisy. I suspect my complaints about this should be aimed at inefficient websites and Microsoft for background Windows tasks. The bad things are probably acceptable, except for one. The fan noise is acceptable, even with the occasional spikes under normal non-gaming use. The kyeboard is nice to type with, but is kind of squishy. I don't notice it while typing (or maybe I do and I like it?) but it is sort of odd to watch. I don't mean the keys are squishy (well, they are a little squishy) I mean the whole keyboard is squishy. While typing, the keyboard kind of bends inward. I don't think there is anything wrong, and I don't think it is going to break or anything but it is sort of strange to watch. Perhaps this is part of the intended construction. I would believe it is part of the chassis being flexible to absorb impacts. The speakers are anemic. They are very tinny - much worse than other laptops. The speakers fire sideways under the edges of the front of the laptop. There is actually pretty good stereo separation, but this effect is lost if you put anything near the edges. For example, it sounds unbalanced with the laptop at the edge of a table when one speaker's sound waves bounce off the surface of the table and the other one is over empty space. The problem is also there is you use an external mouse, unless you use it away from the speaker. Probably not a deal breaker for most as you will use headphones, but I sometimes like to watch a movie while traveling, and I would not enjoy that on this laptop with the built-in speakers. It didn't have to be like that, ASUS! OK, what's the bad thing? It is the touchpad. It lags something horrible and I have not been able to fix it. It is unusable. It mis-clicks, stops for seconds sometimes, and generally lags almost all the time.It is also plastic-y and rattles and clicks when being used. On the plus side, when it is not lagging too badly, the gestures and scrolling seem to work well. I have used an external mouse with this over bluetooth and a 2.4Ghz dongle, and there is no lag there at all. So it is just the touchpad. This may be fine with you - you might never use it without a mouse - or it might make this a bad laptop choice for you. UPDATE - I found a setting that makes the touchpad problem much less noticeable (but sadly, not completely gone). This laptop has two GPUs - one in the AMD Ryzen CPU, and the second "real" Nvidia GTX 1650 GPU. To use the Nvidia GPU fully, Nvidia software is installed. If you open the NVIDIA GeForce Experience app and go to settings (gear icon) the setting for In Game Overlay is turned on. Turning this off helps quite a lot with touchpad lag. It is unclear to me why only the touchpad would lag with this on and not a USB mouse, but it might have something to do with the "I2C HID" connection the touchpad uses; it is not USB and may share a bus with the GPU? However, the touchpad lags when the Nvidia GPU is not being used... ?!? Who knows, perhaps ASUS/Microsoft/AMD will fix this (the touchpad is an "Asus Precision Touchpad" with ASUS drivers on an "I2C HID device" with AMD drivers. I'm sure there are Microsoft drivers involved there somewhere too! I have updated everything already, but as of Fall 2019, the touchpad is unusable in my opinion.

title: Very good money-to-performance ratio. Little in the way of luxury.
text: Probably one of the best sub-$1K laptops I've ever used. Since I don't do a whole lot of actual work on the computer, it's a little unfair to judge it by the merits of a productivity/business laptop. This thing is all gaming, all the time, front and center. Construction is very good. The screen is a matte acrylic/plastic, so it repels fingerprints pretty well. Things like spit or dust do show on the glass, however, so if you talk over a mic regularly, try to say it rather than spray it. Perfomance is nothing short of excellent for a $650 list price. Apex Legends is a consistent 60+ FPS on high settings. League of Legends regularly goes over 100. Skyrim Special Edition is 60 FPS on maximum settings, with a healthy helping of mods, to boot. I don't really have the disc space to try anything else, though; one of the compromises in price was a measly 256G SSD. Fast, but small. I recommend a Seagate Firecuda SSHD for anyone seeking to upgrade. Extra slots for drives and ram are abound, giving this book just enough upgradability to keep you in the gaming scene for a few more years than some of its competitors. It also, blessedly, has all of the I/O on the SAME SIDE. All three USB ports, the HDMI port, the Ethernet port, the headphone jack, AND the charging port are all tucked towards the rear of the case on the left side. It irritates me to no end when a laptop splits its I/O between each side because hooking up all my peripherals makes it seem like I'm playing games on an iron lung. There are, of course, some problems! ASUS Armoury Crate is fraught with software issues. Out of the box, I had to flash the thing and reset it because AC was hard locking the system whenever it changed to "Performance" settings. It also refused to sync the RGB keyboard to any non-default settings for nearly a day, until the RGB suddenly and inexplicably decided it was time to work. It also won't automatically adjust the way it's advertised to, unless the charger unplugs itself, in which case it goes into "Silent" mode. Also, it's bundled with McAfee security, which is akin to going to the doctor and having your insurance plan cover a leech treatment. The battery life is also pretty pathetic; 3.5 hours on "Turbo" settings, sitting idle. Not much mobile productivity. But these quibbles are, ultimately, minor ones. After the reset it's worked like a dream and played every game I've thrown at it. The merely average features are thus: a capable soundcard, a 1080P 120hz screen, a proven but not-extraordinary GTX1650, and the six-core variant of the Ryzen 5. Good enough for most games that are already out and many that are coming out currently. My final thoughts: an excellent gaming laptop at an excellent price. If you've got the cash to drop on one of the MSIs or a Razer Blade, you can, but this cuts the market up pretty cleanly. Good job, ASUS. If only your software didn't gargle bollocks.

Also, they use a single 8GB SODIMM rather than utilizing dual channel with a 2x4GB set, which in theory gives the ability to add another 8GB down the line, but with the original module only running at max 2666 Mhz, you'd be better off buying faster memory anyways. title: Died in 18 months
text: Update: I've had this laptop for about a year and a half and it just bricked. I was in the middle of working on a document and with no warning it turned off and won't turn back on. It was not hot at the time. I took the back off and nothing is loose. It's possible it is the power cable, but I believe I would have noticed the battery going to zero so my next guess is that the board is dead. Naturally my warranty expired 4 months ago. In sum, I can no longer recommend this laptop. Prior to this computer I had an ASUS gaming laptop that was 3 times the price of this one. I was very happy with it, I've had it for 7 years and it's still able to run MMOs, albeit at low settings. I now have a desktop for gaming and didn't want to invest as much in another high-level gaming laptop, but needed a laptop for work and limited amounts of gaming/videos/etc. Now that I've been working from home for a few weeks (thank you, COVID-19), I've had a chance to spend a good amount of time on this computer. I have not yet tried gaming on it so I can't speak about that - I'll have to come back and update later. I have been working, though, and it's been great, especially for the price. I tend to work pretty RAM-heavily - lots of programs open, lots of browser tabs open - I haven't had any problems at all. I will probably add more RAM at some point anyway, but the amount it comes with is perfectly fine. When watching videos, the screen is nice and crisp with good refresh, but again, I haven't played any games. It seems to stay very cool, which is great as my old ASUS ran a little hot. It's practically silent, which is also nice because my old ASUS fans were a little loud. The keyboard is responsive. The keyboard glow is fun - my kids love it - and it helps me type in low light. The color on the keyboard changes colors and "breathes" - it's fine for me, but I wonder if there's a way to lock it on one color... if there is, I haven't found it yet. It can easily be turned off if it's annoying, though. I do have a few complaints - not big enough for me to subtract a star, but I'd like to mention them nonetheless. 1. The trackpad is left of center. I read other reviews that mentioned this before buying and it didn't sound like a big deal, but it actually is pretty annoying. I, like most people, I assume, use the trackpad with my right hand. Whenever I reach for the trackpad/mouse, it's not where I expect it to be and I end up right-clicking when I mean to left click. I also touch it sometimes with my left hand and end up zooming when I want to just move the mouse. Not a deal-breaker and the fix is obviously to use an external mouse, but I like to have the trackpad option for when I'm traveling with the computer. I'm not sure why they put it to the left of center, but if they had to put it one way or the other, I'd rather it be to the right of center. Notes for next time, ASUS. 2. There are not separate home and end keys. The key is home by default and end with the FN key. I use the home and end keys frequently and having to hit FN to use end is a little annoying. I get that a laptop has limited space, but I would rather have had home and end be primary functions on two of the keys above the numpad and other functions be FN+ functions (I hope this makes sense). Or maybe the plus sign next to the numpad could have been smaller to allow for one more key. There had to have been a way around it. 3. I don't know why, but my space bar has a tendency to double space. I'm a good typist and type on lots of keyboards - I've never had this problem before so I don't think it's something I'm doing, I think it's something to do with the space bar itself. Again, not a huge deal, but just a little gripe. So in summary/TL;DR - Great laptop for the price, a few little tweaks by ASUS would make it even better.

That will allow it to run in duel channel mode and increase the CPU's and integrated GPU's performance by around 20% Buy a second 2.5 laptop hard drive, it has an open bay for it. Once installed the ONLY thing you should do in here is set the "Temp limit cpu" to 80. This will help with thermals so much! Trust me. I see a lot of people on here giving bad reviews saying they are struggling during game-play, that issue is because the laptop will sometimes try to use the integrated gpu instead of the dedicated gpu. This is an EASY fix. Make sure your power settings are set on "High performance", and make sure you are plugged into power. If this doesn't fix the issue. You can go into the Nividia Control Panel>Manage 3d settings>Program settings, then choose your game and select "Use Nvidia High performance graphics"

text: Got this one on sale back in January for less than $700 USD plus Prime shipping. I was pretty impressed with it right from the get go. ASUS' proprietary Armory Crate software lets you manage the cooling system and overall performance, and at max settings, the laptop will start to sound like a jet plane. Noise-cancelling headphones are probably a good idea. Aside from those caveats, and poor battery life (the GTX 1650 can barely run at 25% on battery mode since the battery cannot produce enough wattage for it to run at full capacity) it's a solid little machine if you wanna get into PC gaming with a limited budget. Nice job, ASUS.
